title: Mid-century modern
summary: Warm flat color, cut-paper shapes, and playful type. Post-war modernism with a sense of humor.
lede: The graphic and illustrative side of mid-century modern design (about 1945–1969): flat, overlapping shapes in mustard, burnt orange, teal, and olive on warm paper, simplified figures and objects, biomorphic and atomic motifs, and a loose mix of sans-serif, slab, and brush lettering. This record covers that graphic core. The architecture and furniture of the same name are related branches.

era.note: Wikipedia: popular from roughly 1945 to 1970. Getty AAT dates the wider design style ca. 1933–1965. The name was in use by the mid-1950s and became a label for the period after Cara Greenberg’s 1983–1984 book on 1950s furniture.

attestation.label: Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus: Mid-Century Modernist (300343610)
Batsford: Theo Inglis, Mid-Century Modern Graphic Design (2019)

lineage.note: Wikidata lists Bauhaus under “influenced by” and “based on”. Getty AAT names the Bauhaus as a source of the wider style. Herbert Bayer and Josef Albers, both named in Inglis’s survey, carried Bauhaus teaching to the United States.

lineage.label: International Style
lineage.note: Wikidata lists the International Style in architecture under “influenced by” and “based on”. Wikipedia calls American mid-century modern a reflection of the International and Bauhaus movements, more organic and less formal.

Contemporaries. Interpretation: the Swiss style is the objective, grid-bound branch of post-war graphic modernism. The graphic core of this record is the illustrative, hand-made branch that Inglis surveys (Rand, Lustig, Bass, Flora).

lineage.label: Atomic Age (design)
lineage.note: Wikipedia: design of roughly 1945–1967 that uses atomic motifs and space-age symbols. Its starbursts and orbit shapes recur in mid-century graphics and textiles. Treat it as a branch, not the core.

lineage.label: Scandinavian design
lineage.note: Wikipedia: simplicity and functionality that flourished in the 1950s in the Nordic countries. Getty AAT names sleek Scandinavian furniture as an influence on the wider style.

lineage.label: Googie architecture
lineage.note: Wikipedia: futurist roadside architecture of about 1945 to the early 1970s, influenced by car culture and the Atomic Age. A commercial branch with neon signs and boomerang forms.

grammar.text: Mustard, burnt orange, teal, olive, and brick on cream or off-white paper, with charcoal for type. Colors are flat and slightly muted, as in two- to four-color offset and screen printing.
Flat shapes overlap, and the overlap makes a third, darker color. Registration is loose, and edges can look cut or printed.
Kidney, pebble, boomerang, and leaf shapes, circles and half circles, and atomic starbursts. Figures, animals, and objects are reduced to a few flat geometric planes.
Geometric sans-serif or slab headings next to brush script or hand lettering. Words may bounce off the baseline or tilt. Body text is a plain serif or sans-serif.
One large image or shape group carries the page. Text sits beside it on open paper. Layouts are asymmetric but less strict than a Swiss grid.
Textile-like repeats of small stars, dots, or plant forms fill one band or panel, not the whole page.
In film (UPA, title sequences by Saul Bass), flat shapes slide, cut, and pop into place. Few in-betweens, no depth.

diagnostic: Three or more warm or earthy hues (mustard, orange, teal, olive) appear as flat areas on cream or white paper.
Shapes are biomorphic, circular, or cut-paper, not only rectangles.
Shapes overlap, and the overlap shows a darker overprinted color.
Figures or objects are drawn as a few flat, stylized planes.
A script or hand-drawn word appears next to a geometric sans-serif or slab.
counter: Gradients, gloss, drop shadows, or photographic depth.
Neon, fluorescent, or clashing pastel colors.
Thick black outlines around every shape.
A strict modular grid with only one accent color and no illustration.

confusions.difference: Bauhaus uses the primary triad, elementary geometry, and heavy black bars. Mid-century modern uses warm secondary colors, irregular biomorphic shapes, and illustration.
The Swiss style is objective: grotesque type, a strict grid, photography, and at most one accent. Mid-century modern is illustrative, uses several colors, and mixes playful lettering.
Memphis (1981–1987) uses loud, clashing brights, laminate patterns, and black outlines. Mid-century modern colors are warmer and more muted, and shapes are rarely outlined.
Art Nouveau fills the surface with flowing whiplash lines and plant ornament. Mid-century modern shapes are simple, flat, and separated by open paper.

Flat design is a digital interface style with bright UI colors, icons, and no texture or illustration of scenes. Mid-century modern uses printed, earthy colors, overprint, and illustrated compositions.
Corporate Memphis draws flat people with long limbs and bright, saturated colors. Mid-century figures are more geometric, and the palette is warm and muted.

do: Use a warm cream or off-white ground with charcoal text.
Use three or four flat, slightly muted hues: mustard, burnt orange, teal, and olive.
Build the hero from overlapping flat shapes: circles, half circles, pebbles, and one starburst. Let overlaps darken with a multiply blend.
Pair a geometric sans-serif or slab heading with one brush-script word.
Give panels one or two large rounded corners, like a leaf or pebble, and keep the other corners square.
Use a small textile-like repeat in one band only.
dont: Do not use gradients, gloss, or drop shadows.
Do not use neon, fluorescent, or pure primary colors.
Do not outline every shape in black. Shapes meet by color.
Do not fill the whole page with pattern. Keep open paper around the shapes.
Do not use a strict Swiss grid with only one accent. That points to the International Typographic Style.
